content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/backup

# Backup

Runs `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` right now. Same script the `com.keystone.dailybackup`
launchd agent runs at 09:00 daily — this is the on-demand path for when the Mac was shut at 09:00.

## Run it

Do not pre-check anything. Run first, report after.

```bash
/opt/homebrew/bin/pwsh -NoProfile -File ~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1 2>&1 | tail -40
```

Use a Bash `timeout` of at least `600000` (10 min). The memsearch INDEX step is ~75s of a ~85s
healthy run; the default 2-min timeout can survive it, but a grown corpus will not.

## Read the verdict from state, not from the tail

```bash
cat ~/.claude/scripts/logs/backup-state.json
```

`status` is `OK` or `ERROR`; `errors` lists the failed job codes. That file is the authority.
The tail is for diagnosing, not for deciding.

**`status: OK` is not "everything was saved" — read `okCount` too.** A run that skipped the
SSD still ends `OK` with 0 errors. See the SSD gotcha below for what the count means.

## Then clear the stale hook error, if any

A failed run appends a line to `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log`, which is surfaced
as a HOOK FAILURE at every session start. A later successful run does **not** clear it. If `status`
is now `OK` and the file contains only `daily-backup:` lines, archive and empty it:

```bash
cp ~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log ~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log.archived-$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
cp /dev/null ~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log
```

If any non-`daily-backup` line is present, leave the file alone and tell the user what else is in it.
Shell truncation (`: > file`) under `$HOME` is blocked by dcg rule
`core.filesystem:redirect-truncate-root-home`, and there is no `truncate` binary here — use `cp /dev/null`.

## Report

Three lines, plain: did it work, what was skipped, what to do next. Never report "backup complete"
without naming a skipped target — a silent partial backup is the failure this skill exists to prevent.

## Gotchas

**Safe to ignore — expected on a healthy run:**
- `SNAP skip (missing): ~/.codex/memories` — that path has never existed.
- `TARGET baylor deprecated in manifest - snapshots to it SKIPPED` — deliberate.

**Real gaps — always surface these to the user:**
- `TARGET SSD /Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup NOT MOUNTED - orphan and working-tree capture SKIPPED`
  — the run still reports `OK` with 0 errors, but **untracked, gitignored, and uncommitted-modified
  files were not saved anywhere.** GitHub and Google Drive cover only committed and pushed work.
  Tell the user to plug in CRASHBOX and run again. This is the most likely way to lose real work.

  **Cross-check with `okCount`, because the error count cannot see this.** `okCount` in
  `backup-state.json` is the number of jobs that ran, and two whole job classes — `CAPTURE`
  (per-project working-tree files) and `STATE-SSD` — exist only when the SSD is mounted. So:
  - **~31 jobs** = SSD captured. **~9-10 jobs** = SSD was absent; only the 4 `REPO` pushes and
    6 Drive `SNAP`s ran (verified against runs on 2026-09-04 and 2026-09-05).
  - A single-digit `okCount` with `status: OK` is the silent partial backup. Say so out loud.
  - Do not derive this from the error count or the exit code — both read `OK` either way.
- `TARGET ... NOT MOUNTED - is Google Drive for Desktop running?` — the Drive app is not running.
  Start it, then re-run.
- `PUSH ERR ... Could not resolve host: github.com` — a network blip, not a repo problem. Confirm
  with `ping -c1 github.com`, then just re-run; the commits are already made locally and will push.
  (Seen 2026-09-04 09:05: both `global-memory` and `skills` failed this way and a re-run fixed both.)
- `repo-diverged:<name>` — automation will never merge. Reconcile that repo by hand.

**Other:**
- Every log line appears **twice** for launchd runs and once for manual runs. The script both writes
  to the log file and prints to stdout, and the plist captures stdout to the same file. Not a bug —
  do not "fix" it, and do not read doubled lines as two attempts.
- The script is PowerShell only because `pwsh` runs it natively. It manages launchd, not Task
  Scheduler; the Windows original is parked at `daily-backup.ps1.win-orig`.
- `-DryRun` is the only parameter. Use it to preview without writing.

## Examples

**Example 1: routine catch-up**
```
User: "run the backup"
→ Runs the script, reads backup-state.json (status OK, 0 errors)
→ "Backup done, no errors. Everything pushed and copied to Drive.
   CRASHBOX SSD wasn't plugged in, so uncommitted files were not saved.
   Plug it in and run /backup again if you have unsaved work."
```

**Example 2: session start shows a hook failure**
```
User: "the backup failed this morning — fix it"
→ Greps daily-backup.log for the error codes → DNS failure on both pushes
→ Confirms github.com reachable, re-runs the script → status OK
→ Archives and empties .errors.log so the warning stops appearing
```

**What was wrong**

Your progress bars are meant to be `▓▓▓▓▓▓▓░░░`. The file had `â–“â–“â–‘` instead. The arrows `↑ ↓ →` were broken too.

Cause: the file was saved once on Windows with the wrong encoding. Each special character got read as the wrong alphabet, then saved again. So one character turned into three junk ones. 113 characters in total.

**What I did**

1. `~/.claude/settings.json` — repaired all 113 characters. Tested it. It renders correctly.
2. Then I scanned the rest of `~/.claude` for the same damage. Two more files had it:
   - `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` — 8 bad characters **plus a hidden BOM marker at the start**
   - `~/.claude/AGENTS.md` — 25 bad characters **plus a BOM**
3. Repaired both and removed both BOMs.
4. Committed and pushed all three. Your Windows laptop will get the fix on its next `/dev-sync`.

**Worth knowing:** this is the same Windows write that caused your BOM problem on 9/10. Back then only the BOM was caught. The mangled characters were missed and sat there for two days. The BOM is the one that actually breaks things — `dcg` reports a "missing hook" when it sees one.

**One thing to decide:**

Your saved note `project_settings-json-bom-trap.md` only mentions the BOM. It does not mention that the same bad write also mangles every special character, or that `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` get hit too.

- **A) I update that note** to cover both, so next time you check for both together.
- **B) Leave it.**

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/memory-write

# Memory Write

## Outcome
- Fact added to, updated in, or removed from the correct memory tier
- Tier-B caps enforced (2,500 chars for MEMORY.md, 1,375 for USER.md)
- Confirmation: "Saved — will be active from next session."

## Pick the tier first

Ask: "Will this fact still be true and useful in 3 months, across multiple projects?"

**Tier A — `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`** (one file per fact, indexed by MEMORY.md)
- Durable user facts → `user_*.md` (metadata.type: user)
- Stable project conventions / gotchas → `project_*.md` (metadata.type: project)
- Behavioral feedback rules → `feedback_*.md` (metadata.type: feedback)
- External-system pointers → `reference_*.md` (metadata.type: reference)

**Tier B — `~/.claude/global-memory/`** (single capped file)
- Active threads (in-progress work) → `MEMORY.md` `## Active Threads`
- Current env notes (URLs, tool versions, project structure in play) → `MEMORY.md` `## Environment Notes`
- Pending decisions → `MEMORY.md` `## Pending Decisions`
- Durable user profile updates → `USER.md`

## Steps

1. **Decide tier** using the rule above.
2. **Read** the target file in full.
3. **Dedup check** — substring scan; if the fact already exists, skip or update in place.
4. **Cap check** for Tier B — `wc -c < ~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (or USER.md). If over cap, consolidate (merge similar entries, prune stale) before adding.
5. **Write** the change.
   - Tier A: create a new file with proper frontmatter (name, description, metadata.type) and add a one-line pointer to that slug's `MEMORY.md` index. `name:` follows the rule below.
   - Tier B: append under the correct `##` section.
6. **Confirm** in one line: `Saved — will be active from next session.`

## The `name:` field — bare kebab slug

**`name:` = the filename stem minus its leading type token, kebab-cased.** The type
already lives in `metadata.type` and the filename already carries the prefix; repeating
it in `name:` is the third copy.

| File | `name:` |
|---|---|
| `project_automation-cadence.md` | `automation-cadence` |
| `user_sports-teams.md` | `sports-teams` |
| `reference_baylor-house-style.md` | `baylor-house-style` |
| `feedback_project_idea_capture.md` | `project-idea-capture` |

Note the last row: strip only the **leading** token. `feedback_project_idea_capture.md`
is a feedback memory *about* project-idea capture — its name keeps the word `project`.

`[[links]]` target this bare name, never the filename and never a prefixed variant.

This rule exists because it was previously unwritten: an audit on 2026-09-02 found the
corpus split 59 bare / 58 prefixed, which broke 37 links. Both forms look right in
isolation, so without a stated rule the split regrows on every write.

## Actions

- **add** — append (default)
- **replace** — substring match + swap. Preferred over add when updating an existing fact.
- **remove** — confirm with the user before deleting.

## Retrieval — the tiered ladder

When the user asks about past context, decisions, or "did we already…?", climb in order and stop as soon as the question is answered. Do not run memsearch when the answer is already in the injected snapshot.

1. **Tier 0** — scan what is already in context (USER.md, MEMORY.md, today's compiled log). Zero cost.
2. **L1** — `memsearch search "query" --top-k 5`. Hybrid vector + keyword across all indexed paths: Tier A files (including the retired Windows slugs), daily logs, transcripts.
3. **L2** — `memsearch expand <chunk_hash>`. Full markdown section around a hit.
4. **L3** — `memsearch transcript <session_id>`. Raw dialogue. Last resort.
5. **Fallback** — say "I don't have a record of that."

## Daily compiled logs — read-only

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/{YYYY-MM-DD}.md` is produced by `claude-memory-compiler` through its own SessionEnd/PreCompact hooks, and injected by its own SessionStart hook.

- **Never hand-edit these files.** The compiler owns them.
- **Never read them eagerly.** Treat the injected snapshot as the source of truth.

## What is loaded at session start

`~/.claude/global-memory/USER.md` and `MEMORY.md` are read once at session start and are a **frozen snapshot**. Mid-session writes persist to disk but only take effect next session — this is deliberate, to preserve the prefix cache. Never load more than the startup set proactively.

## Rules

- Never exceed Tier B caps. Consolidate first.
- Always dedup before adding.
- For Tier A, the slug is the current cwd with `/` and `.` replaced by `-` (so `~` → `-Users-kristinarash`, `~/DEV` → `-Users-kristinarash-DEV`, `~/.claude/skills` → `-Users-kristinarash--claude-skills`). The harness injects the correct slug each session — use that, don't reconstruct it.
- **Never write to a `C--Users-eric-rash*` slug.** Those are pre-migration Windows keys from the box retired 2026-08-14. They are still indexed by memsearch, so old facts stay recallable, but nothing written there will ever be auto-injected again.
- Never announce the write mid-session beyond the one-line confirmation. The injected snapshot is frozen — the new fact appears next session, not this one.

---
name: settings-json-bom-trap
description: "A UTF-8 BOM in ~/.claude/settings.json makes dcg report the hook as missing — the fix is stripping the BOM, never `dcg install`"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
---

`~/.claude/settings.json` acquired a **UTF-8 BOM** — the 3 invisible bytes
`EF BB BF` at the start of the file. Claude Code parses the file anyway, so
nothing in Claude Code looked broken. `dcg` (Destructive Command Guard) does
not, so it printed at every session start:

```
[dcg] Hook missing from ~/.claude/settings.json — run: dcg install
```

**The message is wrong, and its suggested fix is the wrong fix.** The hook was
present and correct all along, at line 318. Running `dcg install` would have
added a second hook to a file the tool cannot read.

**Diagnose, don't trust the banner.** `dcg doctor` names the real fault:

```
Checking Claude Code settings... OK
Checking hook wiring... ERROR
  Invalid JSON: expected value at line 1 column 1
```

"Line 1 column 1" on a file that is visibly valid JSON means a BOM. Confirm it:

```bash
python3 -c "import json;json.load(open('/Users/kristinarash/.claude/settings.json'))"
# JSONDecodeError: Unexpected UTF-8 BOM (decode using utf-8-sig)
```

**Fix** — back up, strip 3 bytes, re-run `dcg doctor` (fixed 2026-09-10):

```python
p = "/Users/kristinarash/.claude/settings.json"
b = open(p, "rb").read()
if b.startswith(b"\xef\xbb\xbf"):
    open(p, "wb").write(b[3:])
```

**The generalisation.** A BOM is already a known trap on this machine's data
files (the PFF season CSVs need `encoding='utf-8-sig'`). This is the same trap
on a *config* file, and it is nastier there: the tolerant reader is the one you
look at, and the strict reader is the one that complains — about the wrong
thing. Whenever a tool claims a config entry is missing and you can see the
entry, check the file's first bytes before editing anything.

Related: [[dcg-guard-blocks]], [[hook-two-copies-trap]], [[path-shadowing-and-cleanup]]

surface at completely different times, so finding one does not mean you found
both. On 2026-09-10 only the BOM was caught; the mojibake sat undetected for two
more days until the statusline was looked at directly on 2026-09-11.

Claude Code looks broken. `dcg` (Destructive Command Guard) does not, so it
prints at every session start:

[dcg] Hook missing from ~/.claude/settings.json — run: dcg install
```

present and correct all along. Running `dcg install` would have added a second
hook to a file the tool cannot read.

**Diagnose, don't trust the banner.** `dcg doctor` names the real fault:

```
Checking hook wiring... ERROR
  Invalid JSON: expected value at line 1 column 1
```

"Line 1 column 1" on a file that is visibly valid JSON means a BOM.

## Fault 2 — CP1252 double-encoding (silent, cosmetic-looking)

as UTF-8. Every non-ASCII character becomes 2–3 junk characters. Nothing errors.
Nothing warns. JSON stays valid. You only notice by *looking at rendered output*.

box characters:

| Intended | Becomes | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `░` U+2591 | `â–‘` | statusline meter bar (empty) |
| `▓` U+2593 | `â–“` | statusline meter bar (filled) |
| `↑ ↓ →` | `â†‘ â†“ â†’` | git ahead/behind, cache arrow |
| `—` em-dash | `â€”` | CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md prose |
| `…` `’` `·` | `â€¦` `â€™` `Â·` | CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md prose |

read as Latin-1.

carried BOMs that the 9/10 fix never looked at:

- `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` — 8 mangled chars **+ BOM**
- `~/.claude/AGENTS.md` — 25 mangled chars **+ BOM**

Always sweep the whole tree, never just the file that complained.

s = open(p, encoding="utf-8").read().lstrip("﻿")
fixed = s.encode("cp1252").decode("utf-8")   # exact inverse
json.loads(fixed)                             # must still parse
open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n").write(fixed)

where it fails. Sweep for survivors with this scan:

Reason: shell truncating redirect (including arbitrary numeric, named, and PowerShell all-stream forms) to a sensitive system or home path destroys the previous file contents. EXTREMELY DANGEROUS.

Explanation: `> /etc/passwd` (or `: > /etc/passwd`, `echo > /etc/passwd`, etc.) opens the target file with O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC — the contents are destroyed before any write happens. This applies equally to `>|` (force-overwrite), `&>` / `>&` (stdout+stderr to file), and numbered FD forms (`1>`, `2>`, `1>|`, `2>|`). All of these are silent, immediate, irrecoverable.
             
             There is NO recovery without backups.
             
             Safer alternatives:
             - Use append (`>>`) to preserve existing content: `echo line >> <file>`.
             - Make a backup: `cp <file> <file>.bak && echo data > <file>`.
             - For temp scratch: `> /tmp/<subdir>/scratch` is allowed.
             - Read redirects (`< <file>`) are not affected — they don't truncate.

Rule: core.filesystem:redirect-truncate-root-home

If this operation is truly needed, ask the user for explicit permission and have them run the command manually.

`~/.claude/settings.json` acquired a **UTF-8 BOM** — the 3 invisible bytes
`EF BB BF` at the start of the file. Claude Code parses the file anyway, so
nothing in Claude Code looked broken. `dcg` (Destructive Command Guard) does
not, so it printed at every session start:

```
[dcg] Hook missing from ~/.claude/settings.json — run: dcg install
```

**The message is wrong, and its suggested fix is the wrong fix.** The hook was
present and correct all along, at line 318. Running `dcg install` would have
added a second hook to a file the tool cannot read.

**Diagnose, don't trust the banner.** `dcg doctor` names the real fault:

```
Checking Claude Code settings... OK
Checking hook wiring... ERROR
  Invalid JSON: expected value at line 1 column 1
```

"Line 1 column 1" on a file that is visibly valid JSON means a BOM. Confirm it:

```bash
python3 -c "import json;json.load(open('/Users/kristinarash/.claude/settings.json'))"
# JSONDecodeError: Unexpected UTF-8 BOM (decode using utf-8-sig)
```

**Fix** — back up, strip 3 bytes, re-run `dcg doctor` (fixed 2026-09-10):

```python
p = "/Users/kristinarash/.claude/settings.json"
b = open(p, "rb").read()
if b.startswith(b"\xef\xbb\xbf"):
    open(p, "wb").write(b[3:])
```

**The generalisation.** A BOM is already a known trap on this machine's data
files (the PFF season CSVs need `encoding='utf-8-sig'`). This is the same trap
on a *config* file, and it is nastier there: the tolerant reader is the one you
look at, and the strict reader is the one that complains — about the wrong
thing. Whenever a tool claims a config entry is missing and you can see the
entry, check the file's first bytes before editing anything.

# RECOVERY-INVENTORY.md — what would I lose if a machine died today?

Surveyed 2026-09-12 on the Windows laptop (`bu-1979fj4`). This is the cheap version of a
restore runbook: for each category of state, where the second copy lives. Write the runbook
only after the holes below are closed, because a runbook that restores from a backup that
was never taken is worse than none.

`START-HERE.md` is the Mac restore runbook and has been executed once. There is no Windows
equivalent, and the findings below are why one cannot be written yet.

---

## VERDICT

**The Windows laptop has no working automated backup.** Anything pushed to GitHub is safe.
Everything else on this machine exists in exactly one place.

Git coverage is genuinely good: 131 repos, 0 unpushed, 0 without a remote, 1 uncommitted
file at survey time. The gap is entirely in what git does not track.

---

## What IS covered

| State | Second copy | Verified |
|---|---|---|
| Tracked code, all 131 DEV repos | GitHub `erash11` | 0 unpushed, 0 missing remotes |
| `~/.claude` config, hooks, settings | GitHub `dotclaude` | in sync |
| Skills (~160) | GitHub `claude-skills` | in sync |
| Global memory, handoffs, transcripts | GitHub `claude-global-memory` | in sync, both machines pushing |
| Documents and deliverables | Google Drive `00_Primary_Storage_Drive` (G:) | DriveFS, continuous |
| Credentials | Password manager | the only source, by design |

## What is NOT covered

| State | Size | Where it exists |
|---|---|---|
| Gitignored data across DEV | ~15 GB | this disk only |
| `SportScienceResearchRepo` working data | 4.37 GB | this disk only |
| `Football` (non-repo folder) | 2.94 GB | this disk only |
| `Risk_Stratification_Engine` | 1.80 GB | this disk only |
| `ForcePlate_DecisionSystem` (incl. the DB) | 1.69 GB | this disk only |
| Uncommitted working-tree edits | varies | this disk only |
| `~/.codex` session history | large | this disk only |

Some of these have a Mac counterpart from the 2026-08-05 restore, but only as of that date.
Anything worked on Windows since then is single-copy.

---

## Why: three findings

### 1. Every KeystoneOS scheduled task on Windows is Disabled

All nine, `KeystoneOS-DailyBackup` included. They were switched off around the Mac migration
and never switched back on or replaced. Nothing has replaced their function.

### 2. The two replacement tasks have never run

`Backup DEV to Drive` and `Backup AI Sessions to Drive` are registered and report state
`Ready`, which reads as healthy and is not. Both have **no last run time and no next run
time** — registered without a trigger, so they will never fire on their own. Their scripts
were written 2026-09-10 and live in `DEV\_INBOX\`, a staging folder that `dev-sync` skips
because it starts with `_`, so they are not in any repo either.

`Ready` with no trigger is the exact silent-failure shape this stack keeps producing: a
component reports success while the path it belongs to does nothing.

### 3. The backup manifest on this machine is the Mac's

`~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.json` syncs through dotclaude, so Windows has it, but
every destination in it is a Mac path:

```
ssd        -> /Volumes/CRASHBOX/AssistantBackup
transport  -> /Volumes/ASSISTANT/AssistantBackup
drive      -> /Users/kristinarash/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-.../Backups/Machine
baylor     -> /Users/kristinarash/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-BaylorUniversity/...
github     -> https://github.com/erash11
```

## What it says

**Your Windows laptop has no working backup.** Anything pushed to GitHub is safe. Everything else on that machine exists in **one place only**.

It says the two backup scripts sit in `DEV\_INBOX\` and are "not in any repo either" because `dev-sync` skips folders starting with `_`.

- `_INBOX` is its own repo at `github.com/erash11/_INBOX`, clean and pushed.
- Both scripts are on this Mac right now at `~/DEV/_INBOX/backup_dev.ps1` and `backup_ai_sessions.ps1`.

**Give the two Windows tasks a trigger.** They are already written and registered. One `schtasks` change each. That is the whole difference between 15 GB single-copy and 15 GB backed up.

One warning worth keeping: `backup_dev.ps1` uses `/MIR`, which mirrors. If you delete something by accident, a mirror copies the deletion into your backup. Change it to `/E`.

I cannot run `schtasks` from here — it must happen on the Windows laptop.

# Fix the Windows backup — paste-ready

Written on the Mac 2026-09-11, after `~/.claude/RECOVERY-INVENTORY.md` found the
Windows laptop has no working automated backup. ~15 GB of gitignored data on that
machine exists in exactly one place.

Run every block below on the **Windows laptop**, in an **elevated PowerShell 7**
(`pwsh`) window, logged in as Eric. Do them in order.

Already done for you on the Mac and pushed, so `/dev-sync` first to pull it:

- `DEV\_INBOX\backup_dev.ps1` — `/MIR` changed to `/E` (additive, never mirrored)
- `~\.claude\scripts\backup-manifest.windows.json` — Windows destinations recorded

---

## Step 0 — pull the fixes

```powershell
cd $env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\DEV ; /dev-sync
```

Or by hand:

```powershell
git -C "$env:USERPROFILE\.claude" pull
git -C "$env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\DEV\_INBOX" pull
```

---

## Step 1 — confirm the task names

The names below come from the survey and are **not verified from the Mac**. Check
them first. If they differ, use what this prints in every later command.

```powershell
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object TaskName -like "*Backup*" |
  Select-Object TaskName, State, @{n='Action';e={$_.Actions.Execute + ' ' + $_.Actions.Arguments}}
```

Also confirm each task points at the right script. A trigger firing into a wrong
path fails silently:

```powershell
(Get-ScheduledTask "Backup DEV to Drive").Actions
(Get-ScheduledTask "Backup AI Sessions to Drive").Actions
```

Expected: `...\Desktop\DEV\_INBOX\backup_dev.ps1` and `...\backup_ai_sessions.ps1`.

---

## Step 2 — give the tasks a trigger

This is the whole fix. Both tasks are registered and say `Ready`, but they have
**no trigger**, so they will never fire on their own.

Do **not** use `schtasks /Change` — it cannot add a schedule type to an existing
task. Use the PowerShell module.

Two triggers each, on purpose:

- `-AtLogOn` — catches you whenever you sit down
- a time trigger — the regular cadence
- `-StartWhenAvailable` — a slot missed because the laptop was asleep runs on wake

```powershell
# Weekly DEV backup — Sundays 18:00, plus at logon
$devTriggers = @(
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Weekly -DaysOfWeek Sunday -At 6pm),
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtLogOn -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME")
)
Set-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Backup DEV to Drive" `
  -Trigger $devTriggers `
  -Settings (New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet -StartWhenAvailable -ExecutionTimeLimit (New-TimeSpan -Hours 4))

# Daily AI session backup — 17:30, plus at logon
$aiTriggers = @(
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Daily -At 5:30pm),
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtLogOn -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME")
)
Set-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Backup AI Sessions to Drive" `
  -Trigger $aiTriggers `
  -Settings (New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet -StartWhenAvailable -ExecutionTimeLimit (New-TimeSpan -Hours 1))
```

### Why the tasks must run as you, interactively

`G:` is a Google DriveFS **per-user** mount. It exists only inside your logged-in
session. A task running as `SYSTEM` sees no `G:` and writes nothing, with no error
you would notice. Confirm the principal:

```powershell
(Get-ScheduledTask "Backup DEV to Drive").Principal |
  Select-Object UserId, LogonType, RunLevel
```

`UserId` must be your account and `LogonType` must be `Interactive`. If it says
`S-1-5-18` / `ServiceAccount`, fix it:

```powershell
$p = New-ScheduledTaskPrincipal -UserId "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME" -LogonType Interactive
Set-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Backup DEV to Drive" -Principal $p
Set-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Backup AI Sessions to Drive" -Principal $p
```

---

## Step 3 — verify the whole path, end to end

Checking that the task exists is not the check. The report's own conclusion is that
part-checks pass while the path is broken. Check the path.

**3a. A trigger now exists.** `NextRunTime` must not be blank — blank is the exact
failure this is fixing:

```powershell
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object TaskName -like "*Backup*" |
  Get-ScheduledTaskInfo | Select-Object TaskName, LastRunTime, NextRunTime, LastTaskResult
```

**3b. Force the small one to run now** (seconds, not the 15 GB one):

```powershell
Start-ScheduledTask "Backup AI Sessions to Drive"
Start-Sleep -Seconds 45
Get-ScheduledTaskInfo "Backup AI Sessions to Drive" | Select-Object LastRunTime, LastTaskResult
```

`LastTaskResult` of `0` means it ran clean.

**3c. Confirm bytes actually landed.** This is the only step that proves a backup:

```powershell
$d = "G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\05_SYSTEMS\AI_Sessions_Backup\$env:COMPUTERNAME"
Get-Content "$d\_backup_log.txt" -Tail 4
Get-ChildItem $d -Recurse -File | Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum |
  Select-Object Count, @{n='MB';e={[math]::Round($_.Sum/1MB,1)}}
```

You want a fresh `done` line with today's date, and a non-zero file count.

**3d. Then run the big one once by hand** and let it finish before trusting the
schedule. It copies ~15 GB, so give it time:

```powershell
Start-ScheduledTask "Backup DEV to Drive"
```

Check it the same way against
`G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\05_SYSTEMS\DEV_Backup\$env:COMPUTERNAME`.

---

## Do NOT re-enable the nine KeystoneOS tasks

`KeystoneOS-DailyBackup` and its eight siblings are Disabled and **must stay
Disabled**.

`~\.claude\scripts\daily-backup.ps1` is no longer the Windows script. It was
replaced by the macOS port on 2026-08-05 — it uses `rsync` and `$HOME/DEV`, neither
of which is right on Windows. The Windows original is frozen at
`daily-backup.ps1.win-orig` and still points at the Mac's destinations.

Re-enabling those tasks would run the Mac script on Windows and fail. Reviving that
path is a separate job: it needs `backup-manifest.windows.json` wired in first.
The two robocopy scripts above are self-contained and read no manifest, which is
why they are the fix today.

---

## Still open after this

1. **No Windows freshness check.** `stack-check.ps1` is Mac-only (launchd). The
   `backup-state.json` on Windows has said `status: ERROR` since 2026-08-14 and
   nothing surfaced it for a month. `handoff-check.ps1` is the precedent for a
   check that runs on both machines.
2. **`backup-manifest.windows.json` is documentation only.** Nothing reads it yet.
   It exists so the Windows destinations are written down, and so item 1 has
   something to read when it gets built.
3. **No `RESTORE-WINDOWS.md`.** Write it only after the above works. The Mac
   runbook found ~30 discrepancies the first time it was actually executed. An
   unexecuted runbook is a hypothesis, not a backup.
4. **Windows has no local second copy.** CRASHBOX is a Mac-attached SSD. On
   Windows, Google Drive is the only destination for gitignored data.

## The problem it fixes

Your Windows laptop has **no working backup**. About 15 GB there exists in one place only. If that laptop died today, it is gone.

The cause: two backup tasks exist on that laptop, but nobody gave them a **start time**. They sit there saying "Ready" forever and never run.

## What you do

Next time you are on the Windows laptop:

**1.** Run `/dev-sync` there. That pulls down what I wrote today.

**2.** Open this file and follow it:

```
C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\_INBOX\FIX-WINDOWS-BACKUP.md
```

It is written as copy-paste blocks, in order.

## The core of it

If you just want the main fix, this is it. Open **PowerShell 7 as admin**, logged in as you, and paste:

```powershell
$devTriggers = @(
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Weekly -DaysOfWeek Sunday -At 6pm),
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtLogOn -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME")
)
Set-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Backup DEV to Drive" `
  -Trigger $devTriggers `
  -Settings (New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet -StartWhenAvailable -ExecutionTimeLimit (New-TimeSpan -Hours 4))

$aiTriggers = @(
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Daily -At 5:30pm),
  (New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtLogOn -User "$env:USERDOMAIN\$env:USERNAME")
)
Set-ScheduledTask -TaskName "Backup AI Sessions to Drive" `
  -Trigger $aiTriggers `
  -Settings (New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet -StartWhenAvailable -ExecutionTimeLimit (New-TimeSpan -Hours 1))
```

Then check it worked:

```powershell
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object TaskName -like "*Backup*" |
  Get-ScheduledTaskInfo | Select-Object TaskName, NextRunTime
```

**`NextRunTime` must show a date.** If it is blank, it still will not run.

## Why the file has more than that

Three things can still silently break it, and the file walks you through each:

- The task might be running as SYSTEM, which cannot see your `G:` drive
- The task names might be different from what I guessed
